text: Raik 182H: Foundations of Economics University of Nebraska-Lincoln Spring 2024 HOMEWORK 3 Due February 22, 2024, by 11:59pm 1. Linda runs a company that produces and sells doors and sells them in a perfectly competitive market where all firms are identical. In the long run, her firm’s total cost function is 𝑇𝐶 = 𝑄4 10,000 + 5𝑄 + 100 if 𝑄 > 0, and 𝑇𝐶 = 0 if 𝑄 = 0. a. Find equations for the long-run average total cost, long-run average variable cost, long- run average fixed cost, and long-run marginal cost of producing doors. b. If the market price of a door is $100, how many doors will Linda’s firm produce? Show your work. c. Given your answer to part B, is this market in long-run equilibrium? If not, report the price and quantity of doors that Linda will produce in the long-run market equilibrium. Explain your answer. 2. Milk and cookies are sold in perfectly competitive markets. The supply curve for milk is 𝑄𝑀 𝑆 = 2𝑃𝑀 + 60. The supply curve for cookies is 𝑄𝐶 𝑆 = 4𝑃𝐶 + 20. a. Calculate the price elasticity of supply for each good using a change in price from $4 to $6. Which supply curve is more elastic? To find the average just divide TC by q. (((Q^4)/10000)+5Q+100)/Q Average variable cost: (((Q^4)/10000)+5Q+100)/Q Average fixed cost: 0 Marginal cost: 4*Q^3/10000 + 5 100 = 4Q^3/10000 + 5 950,000 = 4Q^3 237,500 = Q^3 Q = 61.9281164815 Set derivative of ATC = 0 (3Q^2)/10000 - 100/Q^2 = 0 (3Q^2)/10000 = 100/Q^2 (3Q^4)/10000 = 100 3Q^4 = 1000000 Q^4 = 333333.333 Q = 24.0281141353 Plug Q back into ATC to find the point where minimum cost is reached (((24^4)/10000)+5(24)+100)/24 = 10.5490666667 The market is not in equilibrium because there was a profit made At $4: 2(4) + 60 = 68 quantity for milk 4(4) + 20 = 36 quantity for cookies At $6: 2(6) + 60 = 72 quantity for milk 4(6) + 20 = 44 quantity for cookies Average change in quantity for milk: (72-68)/((72+68)/2) = 0.0571428571429 Average change in quantity for cookies: (44-36)/((44+36)/2) = 0.2 Average change in price for milk and cookies: (6-4)/((6+4)/2) = 0.4 Arc elasticity for milk: 0.0571428571429/0.4 = 0.142857142857 Arc elasticity for cookies: 0.2/0.4 = 0.5 The supply curve for cookies is more elastic b. Demand for milk is 𝑄𝑀 𝐷 = 80 − 2𝑃𝑀. Calculate consumer surplus, producer surplus, and social surplus in the milk market. c. Demand for cookies is 𝑄𝐶 𝐷 = 80 − 2𝑃𝐶. Calculate consumer surplus, producer surplus, and social surplus in the cookie market. d. Would a price ceiling of $5 in the cookie market benefit consumers? What about producers? What effect would it have on total social surplus? Is the market equilibrium with a price ceiling Pareto efficient? 3. The nations of Gondor and Rivendell are both capable of producing swords (S) and rings (R). Gondor’s production possibilities curve is characterized by the equation 1200 = 3S + 10R. Rivendell’s production possibilities curve is 2500 = 5S + 5R. a. Draw each country’s production possibilities curve with swords (S) on the vertical axis and rings (R) on the horizontal axis. b. (2 points) Which county has absolute advantage in producing swords? Which country has comparative advantage in producing swords? Which country or countries have absolute and comparative advantage in producing rings? Explain your answers. Equilibrium for milk: E price = 5 E quantity = 70 Price when q is 0 = 80 Quantity when price is 0 = 40 Supply when supply = 0: 0 = 2P + 60 -60 = 2P P = -30 Use the stuff in the top right and put it in triangle area equation Consumer surplus of milk: ((40-5)*(70))/2 = 1225 Producer surplus: ((5+30)*70)/2 = 1225 Social surplus = 1225 + 1225 = 2,450 Equilibrium for cookies: E price = 10 E quantity = 60 Price when q is 0 = 80 Quantity when price is 0 = 40 Supply when supply = 0 0 = 4P + 20 -20 = 4P P = -5 Consumer surplus of cookies: ((40-10)*(60))/2 = 900 Producer surplus of cookies: ((10+5)*60)/2 = 450 Social surplus: 900 + 450 = 1350 Maximum price: 40 Regular equilibrium price: 10 Price ceiling: 5 Minimum price when supply is 0: -5 Supply when price = 5: 40 Regular equilibrium quantity: 60 Price when quantity is 40: 40 S R 1 120 400 500 500 Rivendell has the absolute advantage because at every point on the graph they can produce more goods than Gondor. To find comparative advantage, solve for R and S for each city and then find their slope Gondor: Rivendell: R = 120 - (3/10)S R = 500 - S S = 400 - (10/3)R S = 500 - R dR = -3/10 dR = -1 dS = -10/3 dS = -1 Rivendell Gondor Based on these calculations, Gondor has an opportunity cost of 3/10 per ring and Rivendell has an opportunity cost of 1 per ring. This means Gondor has a comparative advantage in rings. Gondor has an opportunity cost of 10/3 in swords and Rivendell has opportunity cost of 1 per sword. Therefore, Rivendell has the comparative advantage in swords. Using the points to the left, calculate the area of consumer surplus and producer surplus Area of consumer triangle: ((40-20)*(40))/2 = 400 Area of consumer rectangle: (20 - 5)(40) = 600 Consumer surplus: 1000 Producer surplus: ((5+5)*(40))/2 = 200 Social surplus = 1200 This is less than the social surplus in part c, so this is not Pareto efficient since there are options that would benefit some people available.
